docs.title: 🔄 Xchange.id: Open Job & Task Exchange for AI Societies.
docs.text:
Xchange is a decentralized task exchange protocol for autonomous Agents and AI systems. It solves the connection problem in distributed problem-solving: deciding how to assign tasks to the right agents in open, dynamic, and large-scale environments.

In Xchange, agents with tasks and agents ready to execute them discover, coordinate, negotiate, contract, and cooperate - creating a fluid exchange of tasks where ownership is not fixed but dynamic and adaptive.

🚧 Project Status: Alpha Not production-ready. See Project Status for details.

docs.title: 🌍 Why Xchange?
docs.text:
In Large scale Multi-Agent Systems (MAS) or distributed AI networks, task handling is not a one-off allocation problem. Real-world environments are dynamic, uncertain, and unpredictable:

  • ⚡ Tasks arrive unpredictably in timing, complexity, urgency, and resource demand. (Open-ended)
  • 🧩 No single agent has all the resources, skills, or complete knowledge. (Diversity)
  • 🧠 Agents differ in skills, speed, specialization, cost, and availability. (Fairness)
  • 📈 Workload distribution becomes uneven (some overloaded, some idle). (Unequal opportunities & Inequity in contribution)
  • 🔄 Failures, interruptions, or shifting priorities force real-time reassignment. (Resilience)
  • 🤝 Optimization opportunities arise when agents swap, delegate, or trade tasks. (Efficiency)
  • 🔗 Many problems require sequenced, decomposed, or collaborative task flows. (Division of labor)

Task Exchange solves this by allowing agents to dynamically negotiate, redistribute, and adapt tasks - improving:

  • ⚡ Speed of Completion - faster results through parallelism and balanced distribution.
  • 📊 Resource Utilization - minimizing idle capacity and maximizing throughput.
  • 🛡️ Robustness & Resilience - reassigning tasks under failures or disruptions.
  • 🌍 Adaptability at Scale - scaling across diverse, evolving environments.
  • 🔄 Optimization & Efficiency - reducing cost, time, and computational overhead.
  • 🎯 Specialization Leverage - matching tasks to agents with unique strengths.
  • 🧩 Collaboration & Synergy - enabling coordinated workflows across complementary agents.

docs.title: ⚙️ How It Works
docs.text:
Xchange provides a protocol-driven negotiation system where agents self-organize around task execution.

  1. Roles (dynamic & temporary):
  2. Manager → oversees the task, tracks progress, processes results.

  3. Contractor → executes the task. (Any agent can switch roles as needed.)

  4. Contracts via Mutual Selection:

  5. Managers announce tasks.
  6. Contractors evaluate and bid for tasks.
  7. Managers review bids and assign tasks to the most suitable contractor.

  8. Contractors can further split tasks into subtasks, becoming managers themselves.

  9. Result:

  10. A hierarchical yet decentralized structure.
  11. Every node can both assign and accept tasks.
  12. No single point of control.

docs.title: 🏗️ Key Features
docs.text:
• Decentralized & Loosely Coupled
  • No central controller or storage.

  • Agents exchange only necessary info (on-demand, not continuous).

  • Contract-Based Execution

  • Task execution = temporary contract between Manager and Contractor.

  • Dynamic Task Reallocation

  • Supports both one-time allocation and continuous redistribution.

  • Adapts as conditions, priorities, or resources change.

  • Resource Allocation

  • Ensures balanced workloads to maximize efficiency.

  • Focus & Prioritization

  • Assigns tasks where they matter most for global system performance.

  • Scalable & Resilient

  • Suited for billions of agents in large, open-ended environments.
  • Handles incomplete, uncertain, or evolving information.

docs.title: 🔑 Why It Matters
docs.text:
Without dynamic task exchange, distributed systems risk: - Overloaded agents & idle resources - Suboptimal allocations that waste compute & time - Fragile performance in the face of failures or shifting conditions

Xchange enables: - Faster distributed problem solving - Efficient & fair resource utilization - Robust continuity under failure - Self-organizing, adaptive, and cooperative intelligence

docs.title: 📡 Core Idea
docs.text: 👉 Task ownership is fluid, negotiable, and adaptive. By treating execution as contracts between agents, Xchange enables: - Resilient cooperation without central authority - Scalable negotiation across billions of nodes - Continuous optimization in uncertain, dynamic environments

docs.title: 🚀 Vision
docs.text:
Xchange underpins a future where: - Agents discover, negotiate, and trade work seamlessly. - Task exchange is the social mesh and communication protocol of distributed intelligence. - Problem-solving is faster, more robust, and self-organizing - a true exchange for intelligence.

Xchange A modular platform for dynamic job submission, task indexing, and agent participation across public and private task networks. DSL-driven, pub/sub-aware, and built for scalable AI and human-task orchestration.

docs.title: Exchange System (Xchange)
docs.text:
Xchange runs one exchange per deployment (EXCHANGE_ID, e.g. demo-exchange) — a task board that accepts tasks, decides which of its registered subjects (agents) should do the work, hands the task off, and records the result. Unlike Orcade (which always runs a fixed multi-subject bidding round), Xchange supports four different assignment modes per task, chosen by the caller at submission time — from a pinned direct assignment all the way up to delegating the whole selection process to Orcade's bidding system. All communication with a subject happens through the same external delegate system used by Orcade, and pluggable selection/evaluation logic is delegated to functions hosted in the same external function registry.

Source of truth for everything in this documentation set:

File Responsibility exchange-db/core/schema.py ExchangeTasks, ExchangeSubjects dataclasses exchange-db/core/crud.py MongoDB persistence for the two collections above, in DB exchange_{EXCHANGE_ID} exchange-db/core/task_assignment.py TaskAssignmentService — the orchestration logic for all four assignment modes exchange-db/core/apis.py Flask REST API (app, mounted via main.py / run_server()) exchange-db/core/functions.py FunctionCaller — thin wrapper for invoking selector/evaluator functions exchange-db/core/agents_functions/ Low-level client for the function registry (AgentFunctions, FunctionsRegistryClient, FunctionCaller) — copied as-is from Orcade exchange-db/core/subject_task.py SubjectTask — client for the delegate system — copied as-is from Orcade exchange-db/core/bidding_client.py BiddingClient — client for Orcade's own bid-job REST API, used only by the bidding assignment mode

docs.title: 1.1 Actors
docs.text:
• Exchange (EXCHANGE_ID) — one Xchange deployment is one exchange. It owns its own MongoDB database (exchange_{EXCHANGE_ID}, see §2.4) and its own set of subjects. There is no cross-exchange query surface — "all subjects in the exchange" always means "every ExchangeSubjects document in this deployment's database".
  • Task (ExchangeTasks) — a unit of work submitted to the exchange. Its task_assignment_type picks one of four orchestration strategies (§1.2); its task_metadata.task_assignment sub-object carries the parameters that strategy needs (which subject, which function, which bid-job fields, ...).
  • Subject (ExchangeSubjects) — a registered agent that can receive tasks. Subjects are plain CRUD records (§3.3) — there is no separate "join the exchange" workflow beyond creating the record. A subject's task_evaluation_function field is only consulted by the open assignment mode.
  • Selector function (function mode only) — an external function, resolved by function_id, invoked once with the task and the full subject list; it must return a selected_subject_id. See §5.1.
  • Task evaluation function (open mode only) — each subject carries its own, via ExchangeSubjects.task_evaluation_function. Called per-subject, in order, until one accepts. See §5.2.
  • Delegate system (SUBJECT_DELEGATE_URL) — the same external service Orcade uses to reach a live subject and get a response back (SubjectTask.submit_and_wait, see §6). Xchange never talks to a subject directly.
  • Function registry (FUNCTION_REGISTRY_URL) — the same external function-hosting service Orcade uses. Xchange resolves selector / task-evaluation function_ids against it via FunctionCaller (see §5), reusing the exact same agents_functions client code as Orcade.
  • Orcade / bidding system (BIDDING_SERVICE_URL) — used only by the bidding assignment mode. Xchange acts as a creator against Orcade's own /bid-jobs API — see §7.

docs.title: 1.2 The four assignment modes
docs.text:
Set on submission via task_assignment_type:

Mode Selection Assignment timing Submission timing direct Caller names the subject_id up front. No selection logic runs at all. N/A (fixed) Background thread function A single selector function picks one subject from the full subject list. Synchronous (blocks the POST /tasks call) Background thread open Each subject's own task_evaluation_function is asked in turn; first "accepted" wins. Entirely on a background thread Same background thread (sequential, not parallel) bidding Delegated wholesale to Orcade: a bid job is opened for the subject set and Orcade's own evaluator picks the winner. Entirely on a background thread Handled by Orcade, not Xchange; Xchange only polls for the outcome 
 direct:    POST /tasks ──► persist task ─┬─► return 201 to caller
                                           └─► [thread] submit_and_wait(subject_id) ──► save task_output

 function:  POST /tasks ──► persist task ──► call selector function (blocking)
                                           ├─► return 201 to caller (status="assigned")
                                           └─► [thread] submit_and_wait(selected_subject_id) ──► save task_output

 open:      POST /tasks ──► persist task ──► return 201 to caller
                                           └─► [thread] for each subject:
                                                          call subject.task_evaluation_function
                                                          if "accepted" → submit_and_wait(subject_id) ──► save task_output; stop
                                                          if none accept → status="rejected"

 bidding:   POST /tasks ──► persist task ──► return 201 to caller
                                           └─► [thread] create Orcade bid job
                                                          poll Orcade for a "bid_winner" task-result
                                                          save it as task_output

Key behavioral notes:

  • POST /tasks always returns as soon as the task is persisted and (for function mode only) a subject has been synchronously selected. It never waits for the subject's actual response — that always happens on a background thread, for all four modes. Poll GET /tasks/{task_id} or GET /tasks/{task_id}/output (§3.4) to find out what happened.
  • function mode is the only mode with a synchronous step. Selecting the subject happens inline inside the request handler; if the selector function raises or doesn't return selected_subject_id, POST /tasks itself fails (400) and the task is marked failed — nothing is submitted to any subject.
  • open mode evaluates subjects sequentially, not in parallel, and stops at the first acceptance. Subject order is whatever ExchangeSubjectsCRUD.list() returns (MongoDB's natural document order — not otherwise guaranteed). If a subject's task_evaluation_function call raises, that subject is treated as a non-accept (logged and skipped) rather than failing the whole task.
  • bidding mode has no timeout. It polls Orcade's /bid-jobs/{id}/task-results every bid_poll_interval seconds (default 5s) forever, until a "bid_winner" entry shows up. If Orcade's own bidding never resolves (e.g. a required subject never bids), the Xchange task sits in task_assignment_status="bidding" indefinitely.
  • task_assignment_status values you'll observe: pending (just submitted, only briefly before a mode-specific handler updates it), assigned (function/open mode has picked a subject, submission thread not yet finished), bidding (bid job created, waiting on Orcade), completed (subject responded, see task_output), failed (an exception occurred — see task_output.error), rejected (open mode exhausted every subject with no acceptance).

docs.title: 2. Schema
docs.text: Both entities are plain dataclasses (exchange-db/core/schema.py) that round-trip through to_dict() / from_dict() and are stored as-is (no ORM/mapping layer) as MongoDB documents.

docs.title: 2.1 ExchangeTasks
docs.text:
Represents one unit of work submitted to the exchange.

Field Type Required Description task_id string auto Primary key. Generated server-side (uuid4()) by the API if omitted from the request; the dataclass itself has no default. task_assignment_type string yes One of "direct", "function", "open", "bidding" — see §1.2 and §4. task_data any yes The actual work payload. Free-form — sent verbatim to whichever subject ends up handling the task, and to selector/evaluation functions. Not interpreted by Xchange. task_assignment_status string yes Lifecycle state. API default "pending" on submission; then mutated by TaskAssignmentService — see the status table in §1.2. task_metadata object no ({}) Free-form metadata. Its task_assignment sub-key carries mode-specific parameters (subject_id for direct, function_id/parameters for function, bid_job_* fields for bidding; unused for open). bidding mode also writes task_metadata.bid_job_id back onto this object once the bid job is created. taski_creation_time datetime (ISO-8601 string over the wire) auto Set by the API to the submission time. Note the field name has a typo (taski_ not task_) — this is intentional/as-specified, not a bug to silently rename. task_output object no ({}) Populated once the task resolves: either the delegate system's response (direct/function/open) or Orcade's bid_winner task-result (bidding), or {"error": "..."} on failure/rejection.

Example — full ExchangeTasks document (direct mode, completed):

{
  "task_id": "3f9c6d2e-1a2b-4c3d-9e8f-7a6b5c4d3e2f",
  "task_assignment_type": "direct",
  "task_data": {"instruction": "summarize this document", "doc_url": "https://..."},
  "task_assignment_status": "completed",
  "task_metadata": {
    "task_assignment": {"subject_id": "agent-summarizer-01"}
  },
  "taski_creation_time": "2026-09-17T10:15:32.481203",
  "task_output": {"summary": "...", "acknowledged": true}
}

Example — bidding mode, in flight:

{
  "task_id": "6b1a2c3d-4e5f-6789-0abc-def012345678",
  "task_assignment_type": "bidding",
  "task_data": {"task_type": "translate_document", "word_count": 4200},
  "task_assignment_status": "bidding",
  "task_metadata": {
    "task_assignment": {
      "bid_job_evaluator_id": "lowest-cost-evaluator:1.0-stable",
      "bid_job_pqt_id": "min-confidence-pqt:1.0-stable",
      "bid_job_subject_ids": ["agent-translator-01", "agent-translator-02"]
    },
    "bid_job_id": "8f14e45f-ceea-4a19-8f6e-8b5a9c1a9f10"
  },
  "taski_creation_time": "2026-09-17T10:20:00.000000",
  "task_output": {}
}

docs.title: 2.2 ExchangeSubjects
docs.text:
Represents one agent registered with this exchange.

Field Type Required Description subject_id string auto Primary key. Generated server-side (uuid4()) by the API if omitted. subject_metadata object no ({}) Free-form metadata about the subject (capabilities summary, owner, tags, ...). Not interpreted by Xchange itself. task_evaluation_function string no ("") function_id in the function registry, invoked by open-mode assignment to ask this subject whether it accepts a given task. Empty string means this subject is skipped entirely during open evaluation (see §4.3). subject_capabilities object no ({}) Free-form description of what the subject can do. Passed through to selector/evaluation functions as part of the subject's to_dict(); not filtered or matched against task requirements by Xchange itself. topics array<string> no ([]) Tags used only by bidding-mode assignment to narrow the default subject pool for a bid job — see §4.4 and §7.2. Not consulted by any other assignment mode.

Example — full ExchangeSubjects document:

{
  "subject_id": "agent-summarizer-01",
  "subject_metadata": {"owner": "team-nlp", "region": "us-east"},
  "task_evaluation_function": "accepts-if-capacity:1.0-stable",
  "subject_capabilities": {"max_doc_tokens": 50000, "languages": ["en", "fr"]},
  "topics": ["summarization", "nlp"]
}

docs.title: 2.3 to_dict() / from_dict() notes
docs.text:
• taski_creation_time round-trips as an ISO-8601 string via to_dict() (datetime.isoformat()) and is parsed back with datetime.fromisoformat() in from_dict(); a None value passes through unchanged in both directions.
  • All dict-typed fields default to a fresh {} (via field(default_factory=dict)) when omitted from from_dict()'s input — there is no None vs {} ambiguity to handle downstream.

docs.title: 2.4 Storage
docs.text:
Both entities live in MongoDB (MONGO_URL), in a database named exchange_{EXCHANGE_ID} — i.e. each exchange deployment gets its own database, computed at runtime by crud.get_db_name(). This is also why "list every subject associated with the exchange" (§1.1) needs no filter anywhere in the code — every document in that database belongs to this exchange by construction.

Collection Document key used as Mongo _id tasks task_id subjects subject_id

ExchangeTasksCRUD / ExchangeSubjectsCRUD (exchange-db/core/crud.py) expose create / get / list(query={}) / update(id, {field: value}) / delete. update() applies its updates dict as a raw MongoDB $set — including dotted paths like "task_metadata.bid_job_id" — with no schema validation. list() accepts a raw MongoDB filter document, same convention as Orcade's *_db.query().

docs.text: Base path: none (routes are mounted at root). Default port 5000 (run_server() in exchange-db/core/apis.py; the PORT env var set in the k8s manifest is informational only — like Orcade, Flask's dev server itself is hardcoded to 0.0.0.0:5000 in run_server()).

docs.title: 3.1 Response envelope
docs.text:
Every endpoint replies with the same envelope, identical to Orcade's:

// success
{ "ok": true, "data": { ... } }

// failure
{ "ok": false, "error": "human readable message" }

docs.title: 3.2 How to submit a task
docs.text:
POST /tasks

Persists the task, then synchronously calls TaskAssignmentService.assign() — for function mode this includes the (blocking) selector-function call; for every mode, the actual delegate submission always happens on a background thread (see §1.2).

Request body:

Field Type Default if omitted task_id string server-generated uuid4() task_assignment_type string required — 400 if missing task_data any required — 400 if missing task_assignment_status string "pending" task_metadata object {} 
curl -X POST http://localhost:5000/tasks \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "task_assignment_type": "direct",
    "task_data": {"instruction": "summarize this document", "doc_url": "https://storage.example.com/report.pdf"},
    "task_metadata": {
      "task_assignment": {"subject_id": "agent-summarizer-01"}
    }
  }'

Response 201 Created:

{
  "ok": true,
  "data": {
    "task_id": "3f9c6d2e-1a2b-4c3d-9e8f-7a6b5c4d3e2f",
    "task_assignment_type": "direct",
    "task_data": {"instruction": "summarize this document", "doc_url": "https://storage.example.com/report.pdf"},
    "task_assignment_status": "pending",
    "task_metadata": {"task_assignment": {"subject_id": "agent-summarizer-01"}},
    "taski_creation_time": "2026-09-17T10:15:32.481203",
    "task_output": {}
  }
}

The response is a snapshot from the moment of submission — for function mode task_assignment_status will already read "assigned" in the persisted record (fetch it again via §3.3 to see that), but the object returned inline by this call always reflects the in-memory task object as it was right after assign() returned, so check back with a GET rather than trusting this response for anything beyond task_id.

Failure modes:

Status When 400 task_assignment_type or task_data missing from the body 400 assign() raised synchronously — unsupported task_assignment_type, missing subject_id/function_id in task_metadata.task_assignment, or the selector function (in function mode) raised / didn't return selected_subject_id. The task is still persisted, marked task_assignment_status="failed" with the error in task_output. 500 The initial DB insert itself failed

docs.title: 3.3 How to read a task
docs.text:
GET /tasks/{task_id} — full record.

curl http://localhost:5000/tasks/3f9c6d2e-1a2b-4c3d-9e8f-7a6b5c4d3e2f

→ 200 { "ok": true, "data": <ExchangeTasks> }, or 404 if not found.

docs.title: 3.4 How to read task output
docs.text:
GET /tasks/{task_id}/output — just the two fields callers usually poll for.

curl http://localhost:5000/tasks/3f9c6d2e-1a2b-4c3d-9e8f-7a6b5c4d3e2f/output

{
  "ok": true,
  "data": {
    "task_assignment_status": "completed",
    "task_output": {"summary": "...", "acknowledged": true}
  }
}

→ 404 if the task doesn't exist. There is no long-poll / websocket mode — callers are expected to poll this endpoint themselves.

docs.title: 3.5 Task endpoints — full reference
docs.text:
Method Path Purpose POST /tasks Submit a task (§3.2) GET /tasks/{task_id} Fetch one task by ID (§3.3) GET /tasks/{task_id}/output Fetch just status + output (§3.4) POST /tasks/query Query tasks with a raw Mongo filter

There is intentionally no PUT/PATCH/DELETE for tasks in this API — unlike Orcade's bid jobs, task state is only ever mutated internally by TaskAssignmentService, not by API callers.

# every task currently sitting in "bidding"
curl -X POST http://localhost:5000/tasks/query \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"task_assignment_status": "bidding"}'

# every open-mode task that got rejected by all subjects
curl -X POST http://localhost:5000/tasks/query \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"task_assignment_type": "open", "task_assignment_status": "rejected"}'

Because the filter is passed straight to collection.find(), any valid Mongo query operator works ($gt, $in, $exists, ...). No projection support, no auth/ACL layer — trusted-network only, same as Orcade.

docs.title: 3.6 Subjects — full reference
docs.text:
Method Path Purpose POST /subjects Create a subject GET /subjects/{subject_id} Fetch one subject PUT / PATCH /subjects/{subject_id} Raw $set update; 404 if the subject doesn't exist DELETE /subjects/{subject_id} Delete a subject; 404 if it didn't exist POST /subjects/query Query subjects with a raw Mongo filter

Create:

curl -X POST http://localhost:5000/subjects \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "subject_id": "agent-summarizer-01",
    "subject_metadata": {"owner": "team-nlp"},
    "task_evaluation_function": "accepts-if-capacity:1.0-stable",
    "subject_capabilities": {"max_doc_tokens": 50000},
    "topics": ["summarization", "nlp"]
  }'

→ 201 { "ok": true, "data": <ExchangeSubjects> }. subject_id is server-generated if omitted.

Update (unlike Orcade's bid-job update, this one checks existence first and returns the fresh document, not just a modified count):

curl -X PATCH http://localhost:5000/subjects/agent-summarizer-01 \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"subject_capabilities": {"max_doc_tokens": 80000}}'

→ 200 { "ok": true, "data": <updated ExchangeSubjects> }, or 404 if the subject doesn't exist.

Delete:

curl -X DELETE http://localhost:5000/subjects/agent-summarizer-01

→ 200 { "ok": true, "data": {"deleted": true} }, or 404 if not found.

Query — same raw-Mongo-filter convention as /tasks/query:

# every subject that participates in open-mode evaluation
curl -X POST http://localhost:5000/subjects/query \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"task_evaluation_function": {"$ne": ""}}'

# every subject tagged with the "nlp" topic — the same filter
# bidding mode itself uses when a task specifies "topics" (§4.4, §7.2)
curl -X POST http://localhost:5000/subjects/query \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"topics": {"$in": ["nlp"]}}'

docs.title: 4. Assignment modes
docs.text:
All four modes are implemented as branches of TaskAssignmentService.assign() (exchange-db/core/task_assignment.py), called once, synchronously, from inside the POST /tasks handler (exchange-db/core/apis.py). Every mode ends the same way — a call to the private _submit_and_save() helper, which does the actual delegate round-trip and writes task_output / task_assignment_status back to Mongo:

def _submit_and_save(self, task, subject_id):
    try:
        result = self._subject_task.submit_and_wait(
            subject_id=subject_id,
            session_id=task.task_id,
            task_id=task.task_id,
            task_data=task.task_data,
        )
        self._tasks_crud.update(task.task_id, {"task_output": result, "task_assignment_status": "completed"})
    except Exception as e:
        self._tasks_crud.update(task.task_id, {"task_assignment_status": "failed", "task_output": {"error": str(e)}})

The four modes differ only in how subject_id gets decided and which parts of that decision happen synchronously vs. on a background thread. See §6 for what submit_and_wait actually sends.

docs.title: 4.1 direct mode
docs.text:
Config (task_metadata.task_assignment):

Field Type Required subject_id string yes — KeyError (surfaces as the API's 400) if missing

What happens:

def _handle_direct(self, task):
    subject_id = task.task_metadata["task_assignment"]["subject_id"]
    threading.Thread(target=self._submit_and_save, args=(task, subject_id), daemon=True).start()

No selection logic at all — the caller already knows who should do the work. The only asynchronous part is the delegate round-trip itself; POST /tasks returns immediately after the thread is started.

docs.title: 4.2 function mode
docs.text:
Config (task_metadata.task_assignment):

Field Type Required function_id string yes — KeyError if missing parameters object no ({}) — forwarded as FunctionCaller.call(..., parameters=...)

What happens:

def _handle_function(self, task):
    assignment = task.task_metadata["task_assignment"]
    subjects = self._subjects_crud.list()                       # every subject in this exchange
    result = self._function_caller.call(
        function_id=assignment["function_id"],
        input_data={"task_data": task.task_data, "subjects": [s.to_dict() for s in subjects]},
        parameters=assignment.get("parameters", {}),
    )
    selected_subject_id = result["selected_subject_id"]          # raises if falsy/missing
    self._tasks_crud.update(task.task_id, {"task_assignment_status": "assigned"})
    threading.Thread(target=self._submit_and_save, args=(task, selected_subject_id), daemon=True).start()

This is the only mode with a synchronous step: the selector-function call blocks the POST /tasks request. If it raises, or its response has no truthy selected_subject_id, the exception propagates all the way up to the API handler → 400, and the task is marked failed. See §5.1 for the function's input/output contract.

Once a subject is selected, submission to that subject is still backgrounded — same as direct.

docs.title: 4.3 open mode
docs.text:
Config (task_metadata.task_assignment): none — open mode ignores this key entirely; every subject in the exchange is a candidate.

What happens:

def _run_open_assignment(self, task):          # runs on a background thread from the start
    for subject in self._subjects_crud.list():
        if not subject.task_evaluation_function:
            continue                            # subjects with no evaluation function never participate
        try:
            result = self._function_caller.call(
                function_id=subject.task_evaluation_function,
                input_data={"task_data": task.task_data, "subject": subject.to_dict()},
            )
        except Exception:
            continue                            # a failing evaluator is treated as "did not accept"
        if result.get("status") == "accepted":
            self._tasks_crud.update(task.task_id, {"task_assignment_status": "assigned"})
            self._submit_and_save(task, subject.subject_id)     # inline — already on the background thread
            return
    self._tasks_crud.update(task.task_id, {"task_assignment_status": "rejected", "task_output": {"error": "no subject accepted the task"}})

Unlike function mode, the entire flow — evaluating every subject and submitting to the winner — runs on one background thread, started immediately when POST /tasks is handled. Nothing here is parallelized: subjects are asked one at a time, in whatever order MongoDB returns them, and the loop stops at the first "status": "accepted" response. If no subject accepts (or the exchange has no subjects with a task_evaluation_function set), the task ends in task_assignment_status="rejected" with an explanatory task_output.error — this is a normal terminal state, not a bug.

See §5.2 for the per-subject evaluation function's input/output contract.

docs.title: 4.4 bidding mode
docs.text:
Config (task_metadata.task_assignment):

Field Type Required Notes bid_job_evaluator_id string yes — KeyError if missing Forwarded straight to Orcade bid_job_pqt_id string no ("") Forwarded straight to Orcade bid_job_tie_id string no ("") Forwarded straight to Orcade (inert on Orcade's side too) bid_job_metadata object no ({}) Forwarded straight to Orcade bid_job_description object no ({}) Forwarded straight to Orcade bid_job_name object no ({}) Forwarded straight to Orcade bid_job_creator_id string no ("") Forwarded straight to Orcade bid_job_subject_ids array<string> no Explicit subject list. topics array<string> no Resolved to every ExchangeSubjects whose own topics list intersects this one ({"topics": {"$in": topics}}). bid_job_mode string no ("closed") "closed" (default), "open", or "mixed". Open and mixed modes are described below. bid_job_max_subjects integer open mode Forwarded to Orcade; job closes once this many subjects have applied. bid_job_max_time integer (seconds) open mode Forwarded to Orcade; job closes this many seconds after creation. bid_job_tags array<string> no ([]) Forwarded to Orcade. Subjects discover open jobs by these tags.

Open mode (bid_job_mode: "open"). Subjects are not pre-selected: they find the job on Orcade by bid_job_tags and apply themselves. Orcade closes the job on bid_job_max_subjects or bid_job_max_time (or whichever comes first) and evaluates the applicants. Consequently, open mode rejects bid_job_subject_ids and topics synchronously (400 from POST /tasks), since neither has meaning there. Xchange's poller also stops early with task_assignment_status="rejected" if the job closes with no applicants, instead of waiting forever.

Mixed mode (bid_job_mode: "mixed"). A fixed, required roster like closed mode — Orcade rejects a mixed-mode job with an empty bid_job_subject_ids — but Orcade also auto-tags each named subject with subject::<subject_id> on top of any bid_job_tags you supply, so a subject can discover the job by tag (matching its own ID) as a fallback or alternative to receiving the bid_request push notification. Both are still sent in mixed mode — see Orcade's schema doc for the tagging mechanics. From Xchange's side, mixed behaves identically to closed: only bid_job_mode == "open" changes how the subject pool and the polling loop are handled (see the code below), so bid_job_subject_ids / topics resolution, bid_job_max_subjects / bid_job_max_time (which do not apply here — Orcade rejects them for anything but open), and the no-early-exit polling behavior are all exactly as described for closed below.

For both closed and mixed: if both bid_job_subject_ids and topics are given, the final subject pool is their union (deduplicated, order-preserving) — not an intersection and not one taking priority over the other. If only one is given, that one alone determines the pool. If neither is given, the pool defaults to every subject in this exchange (ExchangeSubjectsCRUD.list()) — for mixed mode this also satisfies Orcade's "at least one subject" requirement as long as the exchange isn't empty; if it is, job creation fails on Orcade's side and the task is marked failed, the same way any other Orcade-side validation failure is handled (e.g. a subject ID containing a comma).

What happens: the entire thing — job creation and polling for a result — runs on one background thread, started immediately when POST /tasks is handled:

def _run_bidding(self, task):
    assignment = task.task_metadata["task_assignment"]
    explicit_subject_ids = assignment.get("bid_job_subject_ids") or []
    topics = assignment.get("topics")
    topic_subject_ids = (
        [s.subject_id for s in self._subjects_crud.list({"topics": {"$in": topics}})]
        if topics else []
    )

    if explicit_subject_ids or topic_subject_ids:
        subject_ids = list(dict.fromkeys(explicit_subject_ids + topic_subject_ids))
    else:
        subject_ids = [s.subject_id for s in self._subjects_crud.list()]

    bid_job = self._bidding_client.create_bid_job(
        bid_job_evaluator_id=assignment["bid_job_evaluator_id"],
        bid_job_subject_ids=subject_ids,
        # ... other bid_job_* fields, all with defaults
    )
    self._tasks_crud.update(task.task_id, {
        "task_metadata.bid_job_id": bid_job["bid_job_id"],
        "task_assignment_status": "bidding",
    })

    while True:
        task_results = self._bidding_client.get_task_results(bid_job["bid_job_id"])
        winner = next((r for r in task_results if r.get("task_type") == "bid_winner"), None)
        if winner is not None:
            self._tasks_crud.update(task.task_id, {"task_output": winner["task_result"], "task_assignment_status": "completed"})
            return
        time.sleep(self._bid_poll_interval)   # default 5s, configurable on TaskAssignmentService

Xchange never calls submit_and_wait itself in this mode — Orcade does the actual subject delivery (its own bid_request and bid_winner notifications, see Orcade's own delegate-system doc). Xchange's role is purely: open the job, then poll until Orcade records a bid_winner result, then copy that result into its own task_output.

If bid-job creation itself fails (e.g. Orcade unreachable, or bid_job_evaluator_id missing), the task is marked failed immediately and no polling loop starts. If creation succeeds but Orcade never produces a bid_winner (e.g. a required subject never bids — see Orcade's own docs), this task's task_assignment_status stays "bidding" forever; there is no timeout. See §7 for the full request/response detail and how to inspect an in-flight bid job directly on Orcade.

docs.title: 5. Functions to write (selector & task-evaluation)
docs.text:
Like Orcade's PQT/evaluator functions, these are not code inside Xchange. They are entries in the same external function registry (FUNCTION_REGISTRY_URL), referenced purely by function_id string, and resolved/invoked through the exact same client code Orcade uses: FunctionCaller (exchange-db/core/functions.py) → AgentFunctions (exchange-db/core/agents_functions/__init__.py), which supports the same three execution modes per FunctionEntry — external (plain HTTP POST), stateful (long-lived deployment, cached per function_id for the process lifetime), and stateless (one-off registry-managed job). See Orcade's own functions doc, §4.1 for the full AIOSv1PolicyRule authoring contract (__init__(rule_id, settings, parameters) / eval(parameters, input_data, context)) — it applies unchanged here, since it's the same registry and the same client code.

Xchange uses this mechanism for two different kinds of function, one per assignment mode:

docs.title: 5.1 Selector function (function mode)
docs.text:
Purpose: given a task and the full set of subjects in the exchange, pick exactly one subject to do the work.

When it's called: once per task, synchronously, inline inside POST /tasks, only for task_assignment_type: "function". See §4.2.

Input contract:

{
  "task_data": { "...": "the submitted task's task_data, verbatim" },
  "subjects": [ { "...": "full ExchangeSubjects.to_dict()" }, "... every subject in the exchange" ]
}

parameters from task_metadata.task_assignment.parameters is also forwarded via FunctionCaller.call(..., parameters=...) — for a stateful or stateless function this arrives as both the parameters argument to eval() and merged into input_data["parameters"]; for an external function it is silently dropped (the HTTP POST body is input_data only, with no parameters key added) — same caveat Orcade documents for its own evaluator calls.

Output contract:

Key Type Required Meaning selected_subject_id string yes Must be truthy. If missing/falsy, TaskAssignmentService raises, POST /tasks returns 400, and the task is marked failed — no subject is ever notified. There is no validation that this ID actually matches one of the subjects passed in subjects; an invalid ID simply fails later at the delegate-system call (_submit_and_save), marking the task failed at that point instead.

Example input:

{
  "task_data": {"instruction": "summarize this document", "doc_url": "https://storage.example.com/report.pdf"},
  "subjects": [
    {
      "subject_id": "agent-summarizer-01",
      "subject_metadata": {"owner": "team-nlp"},
      "task_evaluation_function": "",
      "subject_capabilities": {"max_doc_tokens": 50000}
    },
    {
      "subject_id": "agent-summarizer-02",
      "subject_metadata": {"owner": "team-nlp"},
      "task_evaluation_function": "",
      "subject_capabilities": {"max_doc_tokens": 200000}
    }
  ]
}

Example output:

{ "selected_subject_id": "agent-summarizer-02" }

Reference implementation (AIOSv1PolicyRule, picks the subject with the largest declared capacity, for a stateful or stateless function):

import logging


class AIOSv1PolicyRule:

    def __init__(self, rule_id, settings, parameters):
        self.rule_id = rule_id
        self.settings = settings
        self.parameters = parameters

    def eval(self, parameters, input_data, context):
        logging.info("selector input: {}".format(input_data))

        subjects = input_data["subjects"]
        best = max(subjects, key=lambda s: s.get("subject_capabilities", {}).get("max_doc_tokens", 0))

        return {"selected_subject_id": best["subject_id"]}

Alternative reference implementation (external HTTP mode, is_external=True):

from flask import Flask, request, jsonify

app = Flask(__name__)

@app.post("/")
def select():
    payload = request.get_json()
    subjects = payload["subjects"]

    best = max(subjects, key=lambda s: s.get("subject_capabilities", {}).get("max_doc_tokens", 0))

    return jsonify({"data": {"selected_subject_id": best["subject_id"]}})

docs.title: 5.2 Task evaluation function (open mode)
docs.text:
Purpose: ask a single subject whether it will accept a given task. Unlike the selector function, this is per-subject: it is stored on the subject itself (ExchangeSubjects.task_evaluation_function), not on the task.

When it's called: once per candidate subject, in sequence, entirely on a background thread, only for task_assignment_type: "open". Stops at the first "accepted" response — later subjects in the list are never asked. Subjects with an empty task_evaluation_function are skipped and never called at all. See §4.3.

Input contract:

{
  "task_data": { "...": "the submitted task's task_data, verbatim" },
  "subject": { "...": "full ExchangeSubjects.to_dict() for just this one subject" }
}

No parameters are passed for this call (FunctionCaller.call() is invoked with no parameters= kwarg, so it defaults to None).

Output contract:

Key Type Required Meaning status string yes (compared exactly) "accepted" → this subject wins; the task is submitted to it and evaluation stops. Anything else (including missing) → treated as a decline, next subject is tried. (anything else) any no Ignored by Xchange today; free to add a reason field for your own logging.

Example input:

{
  "task_data": {"instruction": "summarize this document", "doc_url": "https://storage.example.com/report.pdf"},
  "subject": {
    "subject_id": "agent-summarizer-01",
    "subject_metadata": {"owner": "team-nlp"},
    "task_evaluation_function": "accepts-if-capacity:1.0-stable",
    "subject_capabilities": {"max_doc_tokens": 50000}
  }
}

Example output (accept):

{ "status": "accepted" }

Example output (reject):

{ "status": "rejected", "reason": "at capacity" }

Reference implementation (AIOSv1PolicyRule, accepts if the subject's own declared capacity covers the task, for a stateful or stateless function):

import logging


class AIOSv1PolicyRule:

    def __init__(self, rule_id, settings, parameters):
        self.rule_id = rule_id
        self.settings = settings
        self.parameters = parameters

    def eval(self, parameters, input_data, context):
        logging.info("task evaluation input: {}".format(input_data))

        subject = input_data["subject"]
        task_data = input_data["task_data"]

        capacity = subject.get("subject_capabilities", {}).get("max_doc_tokens", 0)
        required = task_data.get("estimated_tokens", 0)

        if required > capacity:
            return {"status": "rejected", "reason": f"requires {required} tokens, capacity is {capacity}"}

        return {"status": "accepted"}

Alternative reference implementation (external HTTP mode, is_external=True):

from flask import Flask, request, jsonify

app = Flask(__name__)

@app.post("/")
def evaluate():
    payload = request.get_json()
    subject = payload["subject"]
    task_data = payload["task_data"]

    capacity = subject.get("subject_capabilities", {}).get("max_doc_tokens", 0)
    required = task_data.get("estimated_tokens", 0)

    if required > capacity:
        return jsonify({"data": {"status": "rejected", "reason": f"requires {required} tokens, capacity is {capacity}"}})

    return jsonify({"data": {"status": "accepted"}})

docs.title: 5.3 Registering a function
docs.text:
Same as Orcade: whatever you write must already exist in the function registry under a function_id before it's referenced (as task_metadata.task_assignment.function_id for function mode, or as ExchangeSubjects.task_evaluation_function for open mode). AgentFunctions.add() is called automatically, lazily, the first time FunctionCaller.call() sees a given function_id, and raises ValueError if the registry has nothing registered under it — for function mode this surfaces as the 400 on POST /tasks; for open mode it's caught per-subject and logged, treated as that subject declining (see §4.3). Registering the function itself happens against the function registry service directly, outside Xchange's own API surface — identical to how it's done for Orcade.

docs.title: 6. How a task reaches a subject via the delegate system
docs.text:
Applies to direct, function, and open mode. bidding mode does not use this path at all — Orcade talks to subjects on Xchange's behalf; see §7.

Like Orcade, Xchange never talks to a subject/agent directly. Every submission goes through SubjectTask (exchange-db/core/subject_task.py) — the exact same class, copied verbatim from Orcade — against the same kind of external delegate service at SUBJECT_DELEGATE_URL.

docs.title: 6.1 Transport
docs.text:
POST {SUBJECT_DELEGATE_URL}/api/submit-and-wait

{
  "subject_id": "agent-summarizer-01",
  "session_id": "3f9c6d2e-1a2b-4c3d-9e8f-7a6b5c4d3e2f",
  "task_id": "3f9c6d2e-1a2b-4c3d-9e8f-7a6b5c4d3e2f",
  "task_data": { "...": "the task's task_data field, verbatim" }
}
Field Value in Xchange's usage subject_id the resolved target subject (fixed for direct, picked by the selector function for function, the first accepter for open) session_id the task_id — note this differs from Orcade, where session_id is the bid_job_id and task_id is a fresh UUID generated per call. In Xchange, both fields are always the same value: the exchange task's own task_id. task_id same as session_id — see above task_data the exchange task's task_data, sent as-is — unlike Orcade, Xchange does not wrap it in an envelope object with a "type" discriminator (Orcade's bid_request/bid_winner shape). The subject receives exactly what was submitted in POST /tasks, nothing more.

The call is a blocking requests.post(...) with a (10, 300) second (connect, read) timeout, identical to Orcade — Xchange waits up to 5 minutes for the delegate/subject to respond before the call fails.

docs.title: 6.2 What Xchange does with the subject's response
docs.text:
Whatever JSON the delegate returns becomes task_output verbatim, and task_assignment_status is set to "completed":

result = self._subject_task.submit_and_wait(subject_id=subject_id, session_id=task.task_id, task_id=task.task_id, task_data=task.task_data)
self._tasks_crud.update(task.task_id, {"task_output": result, "task_assignment_status": "completed"})

Nothing in TaskAssignmentService reads specific fields back out of this response — there's no "subject declined" branch once submission has started (declining only happens before submission, in open mode's evaluation step, via the separate task-evaluation function call, see §5.2).

If the delegate call raises (timeout, non-2xx, connection error), the error is logged, task_assignment_status is set to "failed", and task_output becomes {"error": "<exception message>"}. There is no retry mechanism — same as Orcade.

docs.title: 7. Bidding mode integration
docs.text: bidding mode makes Xchange act as a creator against Orcade's own /bid-jobs REST API (see Orcade's APIs doc), via a small client — BiddingClient (exchange-db/core/bidding_client.py) — rather than reimplementing any bidding/evaluation logic locally. Everything about how a bid job actually resolves (subject eligibility, PQT rejection, evaluator semantics, the bid_request/bid_winner delegate notifications) is Orcade's behavior, documented in full in Orcade's own docs — this page only covers the Xchange-side glue.

docs.title: 7.1 BiddingClient
docs.text:
class BiddingClient:
    def __init__(self, *, base_url=None, timeout=(10, 30)):
        self.base_url = (base_url or os.environ["BIDDING_SERVICE_URL"]).rstrip("/")
        ...

    def create_bid_job(self, **kwargs) -> dict: ...      # POST /bid-jobs
    def get_bid_job(self, bid_job_id) -> dict: ...        # GET /bid-jobs/{id}
    def get_bids(self, bid_job_id) -> list: ...           # GET /bid-jobs/{id}/bids
    def get_task_results(self, bid_job_id) -> list: ...   # GET /bid-jobs/{id}/task-results

Base URL comes from BIDDING_SERVICE_URL (in the k8s manifest, Orcade's in-cluster service DNS). Each method unwraps Orcade's {"ok": ..., "data"/"error": ...} envelope itself and raises RuntimeError(error) on "ok": false, or lets requests' own HTTPError propagate on a transport-level failure (non-2xx, timeout, connection error) — either way, the caller in TaskAssignmentService catches Exception broadly, so both failure shapes are handled identically.

docs.title: 7.2 Creating the bid job
docs.text:
From _run_bidding(), on the background thread started for the task:

bid_job = self._bidding_client.create_bid_job(
    bid_job_metadata=assignment.get("bid_job_metadata", {}),
    bid_job_description=assignment.get("bid_job_description", {}),
    bid_job_name=assignment.get("bid_job_name", {}),
    bid_job_evaluator_id=assignment["bid_job_evaluator_id"],
    bid_job_pqt_id=assignment.get("bid_job_pqt_id", ""),
    bid_job_tie_id=assignment.get("bid_job_tie_id", ""),
    bid_job_creator_id=assignment.get("bid_job_creator_id", ""),
    bid_job_subject_ids=subject_ids,
)

subject_ids is resolved as follows:

  1. Start from assignment["bid_job_subject_ids"] — an explicit list — if given (the "manually specified" case); otherwise an empty list.
  2. If assignment["topics"] is also given, resolve it to [s.subject_id for s in ExchangeSubjectsCRUD.list({"topics": {"$in": topics}})] — every subject whose own topics field (§2.2) contains any of the requested topics — and take the union (deduplicated, order-preserving) with the explicit list from step 1. Neither field takes priority over the other; specifying both adds their results together.
  3. If both bid_job_subject_ids and topics were omitted entirely, fall back to every subject currently registered in this exchange (ExchangeSubjectsCRUD.list() with no filter).

Note this list is captured once, at bid-job creation time — however it was resolved — a subject added (or re-tagged) afterwards is not retroactively added to an already-created bid job (Orcade's bid_job_subject_ids is fixed at creation, see Orcade's concepts doc).

On success, the returned bid_job["bid_job_id"] is written back onto the Xchange task immediately, so it can be cross-referenced or queried directly against Orcade later:

self._tasks_crud.update(task.task_id, {
    "task_metadata.bid_job_id": bid_job["bid_job_id"],
    "task_assignment_status": "bidding",
})

If create_bid_job itself raises (network failure, or Orcade rejects it — e.g. bid_job_evaluator_id required but this docstring already made it required on the Xchange side too), the task is marked failed and no polling ever starts.

docs.title: 7.2a Open mode
docs.text:
With bid_job_mode: "open", _run_bidding skips subject resolution entirely and sends bid_job_subject_ids=[] together with bid_job_mode, bid_job_max_subjects, bid_job_max_time, and bid_job_tags. Orcade does not notify anyone on creation; subjects discover the job by tag (GET /bid-jobs/by-tags on Orcade) and apply by posting a bid.

The poller checks for two terminal conditions each cycle:

  • a bid_winner task-result exists → completed, as in closed mode;
  • the job has bid_job_status == "closed" and GET /bid-jobs/{id}/bids is empty → rejected with "no subject applied to the bid job". Bids are persisted before a subject claims its slot, so an empty bid list on a closed job means no one ever applied.

A closed job that has applicants but no bid_winner (for example, the evaluator failed) still polls indefinitely, as in closed mode.

docs.title: 7.2b Mixed mode
docs.text: bid_job_mode: "mixed" needs no special casing in _run_bidding — the subject-pool-resolution branch only skips for bid_job_mode == "open", and every other mode (including "mixed") goes through the exact same bid_job_subject_ids / topics union logic as closed (§7.2). The only difference happens entirely on Orcade's side: Orcade requires a non-empty roster for mixed mode (empty → create-job failure → Xchange task marked failed, same as any other Orcade-side rejection), sends bid_request to every named subject just like closed mode, and additionally tags the job with subject::<subject_id> for each one, so a subject can also find it via GET /bid-jobs/by-tags instead of relying on the push notification. Xchange itself never queries by tag — that lookup is something a subject does against Orcade directly, outside Xchange's own flow. bid_job_max_subjects / bid_job_max_time do not apply to mixed mode; if set, Orcade rejects the job the same way it would for closed. Polling behaves exactly like closed mode too — no early "no applicants" exit, since mixed mode has no open/closed application window.

docs.title: 7.3 Polling for the result
docs.text:
while True:
    task_results = self._bidding_client.get_task_results(bid_job_id)
    winner = next((r for r in task_results if r.get("task_type") == "bid_winner"), None)
    if winner is not None:
        self._tasks_crud.update(task.task_id, {"task_output": winner["task_result"], "task_assignment_status": "completed"})
        return
    time.sleep(self._bid_poll_interval)

get_task_results maps to Orcade's GET /bid-jobs/{id}/task-results, which returns every delegate round-trip for the job — both bid_request (one per subject, sent immediately on job creation) and bid_winner (one, sent once Orcade's evaluator has resolved a winner). Xchange only cares about the bid_winner entry; winner["task_result"] is Orcade's BidTaskResult.task_result — i.e. the winning subject's raw response to the bid_winner delegate notification, not the evaluator's own result_data output. If you need the evaluator's result_data (agreed price, rationale, etc.) in task_output too, either have the evaluator function embed it into what gets sent to the subject (so it round-trips back through the subject's response), or extend _run_bidding to also fetch it — Orcade doesn't expose the evaluator's raw output via any endpoint, only via what it forwards to the winning subject (see Orcade's delegate-system doc, §5.3).

Failure/liveness notes:

  • A transient error from get_task_results (Orcade briefly unreachable) does not fail the task — it's logged and the loop just retries after bid_poll_interval seconds (default 5s, set via TaskAssignmentService(bid_poll_interval=...)).
  • There is no timeout on the loop itself. If the bid job never produces a bid_winner (per Orcade's own rules: evaluation only fires once every subject in bid_job_subject_ids has bid — see Orcade's concepts doc), this Xchange task sits in task_assignment_status="bidding" forever. To debug a stuck job, use the bid_job_id written to task_metadata.bid_job_id and query Orcade directly: GET {BIDDING_SERVICE_URL}/bid-jobs/{bid_job_id}/bids to see who has/hasn't bid yet.

docs.title: Jobs Gateway
docs.text:
One Xchange deployment is one exchange: an exchange-db instance with its own EXCHANGE_ID, its own MongoDB database and its own subjects (see the Exchange System docs). An exchange-db instance knows nothing about any other exchange. The jobs gateway is the layer that sits in front of all of them:

  • Registry. Each exchange-db instance is registered once, under its EXCHANGE_ID, with the base URL it can be reached at, plus tags and free-form metadata.
  • Discovery. Callers find exchanges by registry fields (tags, status, any raw Mongo filter), and optionally by what the exchanges' subjects look like. The gateway sends the subject question to every candidate exchange's own /subjects/query at the same time and returns only the exchanges with matches.
  • Gateway. Any exchange-db API call can be sent to /exchanges/{exchange_id}/api/<path>. The gateway looks up the exchange's URL and forwards the request unchanged, so callers only need to know an exchange_id, never a host or port.
  • Health checks. The gateway periodically probes every registered exchange and records healthy / unreachable on its registry entry, so discovery can skip exchanges that are down.

The gateway never reads or writes an exchange's MongoDB directly. Everything it knows about an exchange's subjects or tasks comes from that exchange's own REST API.

Source of truth for everything in this documentation set:

File Responsibility jobs-gateway/core/schema.py ExchangeEntry dataclass and the exchange_status constants jobs-gateway/core/crud.py MongoDB persistence for registry entries, in DB GATEWAY_DB_NAME (default xchange_gateway) jobs-gateway/core/exchange_client.py ExchangeClient: HTTP client for exchange-db (health probe, subject query, request forwarding) jobs-gateway/core/discovery.py DiscoveryService: registry filtering plus parallel subject fan-out jobs-gateway/core/health.py HealthChecker: on-demand and background health checks jobs-gateway/core/apis.py Flask REST API (app, started via main.py / run_server()) k8s/jobs-gateway.yaml Kubernetes Deployment + NodePort Service

docs.title: Contents
docs.text:
1. Concepts: what the gateway is for, how it relates to exchange-db, and what it deliberately doesn't do
  2. Schema: ExchangeEntry field reference, sample document, storage
  3. APIs: full REST reference for registry, health-check and gateway forwarding
  4. Discovery: POST /discover in detail, with registry filters, subject fan-out and the response shape
  5. Health checks: how an exchange is probed and what exchange_status means
  6. Deployment & walkthrough: environment variables, Kubernetes, and an end-to-end example

docs.title: 1. Concepts
docs.text: ← Back to index

docs.title: 1.1 Actors
docs.text:
• Exchange (exchange-db instance): one deployment of the exchange service, identified by its EXCHANGE_ID env var. It owns its tasks and subjects and serves the REST API documented in Exchange System §3. Exchanges don't know the gateway exists. Nothing in exchange-db calls the gateway.
  • Registry entry (ExchangeEntry): the gateway's record of one exchange: its exchange_id, the base URL it's reachable at (exchange_api_url), tags, free-form metadata and the latest health-check result. See §2.
  • Jobs gateway: a single stateless Flask service plus its own MongoDB database (GATEWAY_DB_NAME, default xchange_gateway) holding the registry. It plays three roles, described below.
  • Caller: anything that wants to work with exchanges without knowing where they run: an agent, an orchestrator, a UI, another service.

docs.title: 1.2 The three roles
docs.text:
┌───────────────────────── jobs-gateway ─────────────────────────┐
                          │                                                                │
 caller ── /exchanges ───►│  Registry   ── CRUD ──► Mongo: xchange_gateway.exchanges       │
                          │                                                                │
 caller ── /discover ────►│  Discovery  ── filter registry ──► candidates                  │
                          │               └─ (optional) POST /subjects/query ──────────────┼──► exchange-db A
                          │                  to every candidate, in parallel ──────────────┼──► exchange-db B
                          │                                                                │
 caller ── /exchanges/{id}/api/<path> ──► Gateway ── look up URL ── forward as-is ─────────┼──► exchange-db {id}
                          │                                                                │
                          │  HealthChecker (background, every HEALTH_CHECK_INTERVAL s) ────┼──► every exchange-db
                          └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Registry. Plain CRUD over ExchangeEntry records, plus a raw-Mongo-filter query endpoint, following the same conventions as exchange-db's own subject CRUD. Registration probes the exchange first and refuses to register one it can't reach, unless the caller passes skip_health_check: true. See §3.2.

Discovery. Answers "which exchanges should I send this work to?". It works in two stages:

  1. Filter the registry by tags, status and/or any raw Mongo filter. This step is local and costs nothing.
  2. Optionally, ask each remaining exchange which of its subjects match a subject filter (for example topics containing "summarization"). Only exchanges with at least one match are returned, each listing the IDs of its matching subjects.

Stage 2 is the only place the gateway joins data across exchanges. See §4.

Gateway. /exchanges/{exchange_id}/api/<path> forwards any method, query string and body to {exchange_api_url}/<path> and returns the exchange's response untouched: same status code, same {"ok": ..., "data"/"error": ...} envelope. Anything you can do against an exchange-db directly you can do through the gateway by exchange_id. See §3.3.

docs.title: 1.3 Exchange status
docs.text:
Every registry entry carries an exchange_status:

Value Meaning unknown Never checked. This happens when the entry was registered with skip_health_check: true, or its exchange_api_url was just changed and the background checker hasn't run yet. healthy The most recent health probe got a valid exchange-db response. unreachable The most recent probe failed. The reason is in last_health_check_error.

Status is informational. It never blocks anything on its own: the gateway still forwards requests to an unreachable exchange, and discovery still returns it unless you filter with "status": "healthy". See §5.

docs.title: 1.4 What the gateway does not do
docs.text:
• No provisioning. It doesn't deploy exchange-db instances. Deploy one (e.g. k8s/deploy.yaml) and then register it.
  • No self-registration. exchange-db doesn't register itself on startup. Registration is an explicit POST /exchanges call, made by whoever deployed the exchange.
  • No routing decisions on task submission. The gateway never picks an exchange for you when you submit a task. Use /discover to choose, then submit through /exchanges/{id}/api/tasks.
  • No caching or aggregation of tasks. Task state lives only in each exchange. To find a task, you need to know which exchange it was submitted to.
  • No auth/ACL layer. It is meant for trusted networks only, like exchange-db and Orcade.

docs.title: 2. Schema
docs.text: ← Back to index

docs.title: 2. Schema
docs.text: The registry has a single entity, a plain dataclass (jobs-gateway/core/schema.py) that round-trips through to_dict() / from_dict() and is stored as-is as a MongoDB document. It follows the same conventions as exchange-db's ExchangeTasks / ExchangeSubjects.

docs.title: 2.1 ExchangeEntry
docs.text:
Represents one registered exchange-db instance.

Field Type Required Description exchange_id string yes Primary key. It should equal the exchange's own EXCHANGE_ID env var, though the gateway doesn't verify that. It cannot be changed after registration. exchange_api_url string yes Base URL of the exchange's REST API, e.g. http://demo-exchange-svc.exchanges.svc.cluster.local:5000. A trailing / is stripped on write. Every gateway → exchange call is built from this. exchange_name string no ("") Human-readable name. Not interpreted. exchange_description string no ("") Free-text description. Not interpreted. exchange_tags array<string> no ([]) Tags used by discovery's tags filter ({"exchange_tags": {"$in": tags}}), see §4.2. exchange_metadata object no ({}) Free-form metadata (owner, region, cost tier, ...). Queryable with dotted paths through /exchanges/query or discovery's query. Not interpreted by the gateway. exchange_status string server-managed "unknown", "healthy" or "unreachable", see §1.3. registration_time datetime (ISO-8601 string over the wire) server-managed Set once, when the entry is created. last_health_check_time datetime (ISO-8601) or null server-managed Time of the most recent probe, or null if none has run. last_health_check_error string server-managed Error from the most recent failed probe, or "" after a successful one.

Server-managed fields (exchange_status, registration_time, last_health_check_time, last_health_check_error) are silently dropped if a caller sends them in POST /exchanges or PUT/PATCH /exchanges/{id}. Only the gateway's own health checks write them.

Example: full ExchangeEntry document:

{
  "exchange_id": "demo-exchange",
  "exchange_api_url": "http://demo-exchange-svc.exchanges.svc.cluster.local:5000",
  "exchange_name": "Demo exchange",
  "exchange_description": "NLP tasks for the demo org",
  "exchange_tags": ["nlp", "public"],
  "exchange_metadata": {"owner": "team-nlp", "region": "us-east"},
  "exchange_status": "healthy",
  "registration_time": "2026-10-22T09:00:00.000000",
  "last_health_check_time": "2026-10-22T09:41:30.512044",
  "last_health_check_error": ""
}

docs.title: 2.2 to_dict() / from_dict() notes
docs.text:
• registration_time and last_health_check_time are serialized with datetime.isoformat() and parsed back with datetime.fromisoformat(). A None passes through unchanged in both directions.
  • exchange_tags defaults to [] and exchange_metadata to {} when missing, so downstream code never has to deal with None.

docs.title: 2.3 Storage
docs.text:
Entries live in MongoDB (MONGO_URL), database GATEWAY_DB_NAME (default xchange_gateway), collection exchanges, with exchange_id used as the Mongo _id. Because the database name is configurable, the gateway can share a MongoDB server with the exchanges themselves (which use exchange_{EXCHANGE_ID}) without colliding.

ExchangeRegistryCRUD (jobs-gateway/core/crud.py) exposes create / get / list(query={}) / update(id, {field: value}) / delete, with the same semantics as exchange-db's CRUD classes: update() is a raw $set (dotted paths allowed, no schema validation) and list() takes a raw Mongo filter.

docs.title: 3. APIs
docs.text: ← Back to index

docs.title: 3. APIs
docs.text: Base path: none (routes are mounted at root). Default port 5000, which can be overridden with the PORT env var (unlike exchange-db, where PORT is informational only).

docs.title: 3.1 Response envelope
docs.text:
The gateway's own endpoints use the same envelope as exchange-db and Orcade:

// success
{ "ok": true, "data": { ... } }

// failure
{ "ok": false, "error": "human readable message" }

Forwarded calls (§3.3) return the exchange's response body and status code unchanged. Since exchange-db uses the same envelope, callers can't tell the two apart, except for the gateway's own 404 / 502 errors described there.

docs.title: 3.2 Registry
docs.text: Method Path Purpose POST /exchanges Register an exchange GET /exchanges/{exchange_id} Fetch one registry entry PUT / PATCH /exchanges/{exchange_id} Raw $set update; returns the fresh entry DELETE /exchanges/{exchange_id} Remove an exchange from the registry POST /exchanges/query Query registry entries with a raw Mongo filter POST /exchanges/{exchange_id}/health-check Probe the exchange now and return the updated entry

docs.title: Register
docs.text:
POST /exchanges

Request body:

Field Type Default if omitted exchange_id string required. 400 if missing exchange_api_url string required. 400 if missing exchange_name string "" exchange_description string "" exchange_tags array<string> [] exchange_metadata object {} skip_health_check boolean false. When true, register without probing (status starts as unknown)

Unless skip_health_check is true, the gateway probes the exchange first (§5.1) and refuses to register it if the probe fails. This catches typos in exchange_api_url at registration time rather than at first use.

curl -X POST http://localhost:5000/exchanges \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "exchange_id": "demo-exchange",
    "exchange_api_url": "http://demo-exchange-svc.exchanges.svc.cluster.local:5000",
    "exchange_name": "Demo exchange",
    "exchange_tags": ["nlp", "public"],
    "exchange_metadata": {"owner": "team-nlp", "region": "us-east"}
  }'

→ 201 { "ok": true, "data": <ExchangeEntry> }, with exchange_status: "healthy" and last_health_check_time set.

Failure modes:

Status When 400 exchange_id or exchange_api_url missing 400 Health probe failed. The error reads exchange not reachable at <url>: <reason>. Nothing is persisted. 409 An entry with this exchange_id already exists. Use PATCH to change it, or DELETE first. 500 The DB insert itself failed

docs.title: Read
docs.text:
curl http://localhost:5000/exchanges/demo-exchange

→ 200 { "ok": true, "data": <ExchangeEntry> }, or 404 if not registered.

docs.title: Update
docs.text:
PUT and PATCH behave identically: the body is applied as a raw Mongo $set, so dotted paths like "exchange_metadata.region" work.

curl -X PATCH http://localhost:5000/exchanges/demo-exchange \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"exchange_tags": ["nlp", "public", "fr"], "exchange_metadata.region": "eu-west"}'

→ 200 { "ok": true, "data": <updated ExchangeEntry> }.

Rules:

  • Server-managed fields (§2.1) in the body are dropped.
  • exchange_id can't be changed. A body with a different exchange_id gets 400; repeating the same value is harmless.
  • Changing exchange_api_url to a different URL resets exchange_status to unknown, since the old health result says nothing about the new URL. The next background check, or a manual POST /exchanges/{id}/health-check, fills it in. The update itself does not probe the new URL.
  • 404 if the exchange isn't registered.

docs.title: Delete
docs.text:
curl -X DELETE http://localhost:5000/exchanges/demo-exchange

→ 200 { "ok": true, "data": {"deleted": true} }, or 404 if not registered. This only removes the registry entry. The exchange-db deployment and its data are untouched.

docs.title: Query
docs.text:
POST /exchanges/query takes a raw Mongo filter, the same convention as exchange-db's /tasks/query and /subjects/query. Because the filter is passed straight to collection.find(), any valid Mongo query operator works.

# every exchange tagged "nlp"
curl -X POST http://localhost:5000/exchanges/query \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"exchange_tags": {"$in": ["nlp"]}}'

# every exchange that failed its last health check
curl -X POST http://localhost:5000/exchanges/query \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"exchange_status": "unreachable"}'

→ 200 { "ok": true, "data": [<ExchangeEntry>, ...] }, or 400 for an invalid filter. For combined registry + subject searches, use /discover instead.

docs.title: Manual health check
docs.text:
curl -X POST http://localhost:5000/exchanges/demo-exchange/health-check

→ 200 { "ok": true, "data": <ExchangeEntry> } with fresh exchange_status / last_health_check_time / last_health_check_error. The response is 200 even when the exchange is down; check data.exchange_status. 404 if not registered.

docs.title: 3.3 Gateway forwarding
docs.text:
GET | POST | PUT | PATCH | DELETE /exchanges/{exchange_id}/api/<path>

The gateway looks up exchange_id in the registry and sends the request on to {exchange_api_url}/<path>, preserving the method, the query string, the raw request body and its Content-Type. The response is returned exactly as the exchange produced it, with the same status code, body and Content-Type.

Every exchange-db endpoint (Exchange System §3) is reachable this way:

Through the gateway Forwarded to exchange-db POST /exchanges/{id}/api/tasks POST /tasks GET /exchanges/{id}/api/tasks/{task_id} GET /tasks/{task_id} GET /exchanges/{id}/api/tasks/{task_id}/output GET /tasks/{task_id}/output POST /exchanges/{id}/api/tasks/query POST /tasks/query POST /exchanges/{id}/api/subjects POST /subjects GET / PUT / PATCH / DELETE /exchanges/{id}/api/subjects/{subject_id} same method on /subjects/{subject_id} POST /exchanges/{id}/api/subjects/query POST /subjects/query 
# submit a direct-mode task to demo-exchange, without knowing where it runs
curl -X POST http://localhost:5000/exchanges/demo-exchange/api/tasks \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "task_assignment_type": "direct",
    "task_data": {"instruction": "summarize this document", "doc_url": "https://storage.example.com/report.pdf"},
    "task_metadata": {"task_assignment": {"subject_id": "agent-summarizer-01"}}
  }'

# poll its output
curl http://localhost:5000/exchanges/demo-exchange/api/tasks/<task_id>/output

Gateway-originated errors (everything else comes from the exchange):

Status Body When 404 {"ok": false, "error": "exchange not found"} exchange_id isn't registered 502 {"ok": false, "error": "exchange '<id>' unreachable: <reason>"} Connection refused, DNS failure, or no response within the read timeout

Notes:

  • The gateway never checks exchange_status before forwarding. An unreachable exchange still gets the request. If it has recovered, the call succeeds; if not, you get a 502.
  • Timeouts: (10, PROXY_READ_TIMEOUT) seconds (connect, read), default read timeout 300. That's long enough for function-mode POST /tasks, which blocks on a selector-function call (Exchange System §4.2).
  • One exchange per call. Forwarding never fans out. Cross-exchange queries are discovery's job (§4).

docs.title: 3.4 Gateway health
docs.text:
curl http://localhost:5000/health

→ 200 { "ok": true, "data": {"status": "ok"} }. This is a liveness check for the gateway process only. It doesn't touch MongoDB or any exchange.

docs.title: 3.5 Full reference
docs.text:
Method Path Section POST /exchanges §3.2 Register GET /exchanges/{exchange_id} §3.2 Read PUT / PATCH /exchanges/{exchange_id} §3.2 Update DELETE /exchanges/{exchange_id} §3.2 Delete POST /exchanges/query §3.2 Query POST /exchanges/{exchange_id}/health-check §3.2 Manual health check POST /discover §4 any /exchanges/{exchange_id}/api/<path> §3.3 GET /health §3.4

docs.title: 4. Discovery
docs.text: ← Back to index

docs.title: 4. Discovery
docs.text:
POST /discover answers "which exchanges should I send this work to?" It is implemented by DiscoveryService (jobs-gateway/core/discovery.py) and runs in two stages:

POST /discover
   │
   ├─► stage 1: filter the registry (local Mongo query)            → candidate exchanges
   │
   └─► stage 2 (only if a subject filter was given):
         for every candidate, in parallel:
             POST {exchange_api_url}/subjects/query  <subject filter>
         keep exchanges with ≥ 1 matching subject, sorted by match count (desc)

docs.title: 4.1 Request body
docs.text:
Every field is optional. An empty body {} returns every registered exchange.

Field Type Stage Meaning tags array<string> 1 Keep exchanges whose exchange_tags contain any of these ($in). status string 1 Keep exchanges whose exchange_status equals this, typically "healthy". query object 1 Raw Mongo filter over registry entries, e.g. {"exchange_metadata.region": "us-east"}. subject_topics array<string> 2 Match subjects whose topics contain any of these ({"topics": {"$in": ...}}), the same filter exchange-db's bidding mode uses (Exchange System §7.2). subject_query object 2 Raw Mongo filter over ExchangeSubjects documents, e.g. {"subject_capabilities.max_doc_tokens": {"$gte": 100000}}.

docs.title: 4.2 Stage 1: registry filter
docs.text:
tags, status and query are each turned into one filter and combined with $and:

filters = []
if query:  filters.append(query)
if tags:   filters.append({"exchange_tags": {"$in": tags}})
if status: filters.append({"exchange_status": status})
registry_query = {"$and": filters} if len(filters) > 1 else (filters[0] if filters else {})

This stage only reads the gateway's own registry. It never contacts an exchange, so it's cheap and always available. With no subject filter, the result is simply the matching registry entries, in Mongo's natural order.

docs.title: 4.3 Stage 2: subject fan-out
docs.text:
If subject_topics and/or subject_query is given, they're combined the same way ($and when both are present) into one subject filter. Then, for every stage-1 candidate:

POST {exchange_api_url}/subjects/query    body: <subject filter>
  • Calls run in parallel on a thread pool of DISCOVERY_WORKERS threads (default 8), each with a (5, 30) second (connect, read) timeout. One hung exchange costs at most about 35 seconds on its own thread and never fails the whole request.
  • An exchange with zero matching subjects is dropped from the result.
  • An exchange whose call fails (transport error, non-2xx, or "ok": false) is not dropped silently. It goes into the unreachable list with the error, so callers can tell "has no matching subjects" apart from "couldn't ask".
  • Results are sorted by number of matching subjects, highest first.

Stage 2 doesn't consult exchange_status. A cheap way to skip known-down exchanges is to add "status": "healthy" to stage 1.

docs.title: 4.4 Response
docs.text:
{
  "ok": true,
  "data": {
    "exchanges": [ <ExchangeEntry>, ... ],
    "unreachable": [ {"exchange_id": "...", "error": "..."}, ... ]
  }
}
  • Without a subject filter: exchanges holds the stage-1 entries as-is, and unreachable is always [].
  • With a subject filter: each item in exchanges is a full ExchangeEntry plus a matching_subject_ids array.

400 with {"ok": false, "error": ...} if a filter is invalid, e.g. a malformed operator in query.

docs.title: 4.5 Examples
docs.text:
All healthy exchanges tagged nlp:

curl -X POST http://localhost:5000/discover \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"tags": ["nlp"], "status": "healthy"}'

Healthy exchanges that have at least one summarization subject:

curl -X POST http://localhost:5000/discover \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"status": "healthy", "subject_topics": ["summarization"]}'

{
  "ok": true,
  "data": {
    "exchanges": [
      {
        "exchange_id": "demo-exchange",
        "exchange_api_url": "http://demo-exchange-svc.exchanges.svc.cluster.local:5000",
        "exchange_name": "Demo exchange",
        "exchange_description": "",
        "exchange_tags": ["nlp", "public"],
        "exchange_metadata": {"owner": "team-nlp"},
        "exchange_status": "healthy",
        "registration_time": "2026-10-22T09:00:00.000000",
        "last_health_check_time": "2026-10-22T09:41:30.512044",
        "last_health_check_error": "",
        "matching_subject_ids": ["agent-summarizer-01", "agent-summarizer-02"]
      },
      {
        "exchange_id": "eu-exchange",
        "...": "...",
        "matching_subject_ids": ["agent-summarizer-eu"]
      }
    ],
    "unreachable": []
  }
}

US exchanges with a subject that can handle long documents, combining a registry filter with a capability filter:

curl -X POST http://localhost:5000/discover \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "query": {"exchange_metadata.region": "us-east"},
    "subject_topics": ["summarization"],
    "subject_query": {"subject_capabilities.max_doc_tokens": {"$gte": 100000}}
  }'

docs.title: 4.6 Using the result
docs.text:
Discovery only finds exchanges. It doesn't submit anything. A typical caller picks one entry (the first, i.e. the most matching subjects, or by its own criteria) and then submits through the gateway:

  • direct mode, using one of matching_subject_ids as subject_id;
  • bidding mode, passing matching_subject_ids as bid_job_subject_ids, or the same topics you discovered with;
  • function / open mode, letting the exchange choose among its own subjects.

See §6.3 for a full example.

Matches reflect the exchanges' subjects at discovery time. A subject can be deleted or re-tagged between /discover and submission. exchange-db handles that the same way it would without the gateway (e.g. a direct-mode task to a missing subject ends in failed).
